title: The One With Barry And Mindys Wedding

jokes.text: 'My first girlfriend was Lisa DiBatista. So... I'm no stranger to the mustache.'
jokes.setup: Joey is defending his professionalism about kissing a man, citing past experience
jokes.punchline: The 'experience' turns out to be kissing a mustachioed girlfriend — absurdly specific detail delivered deadpan
jokes.explanation: Exceptionally economical joke. The specificity of 'Lisa DiBatista' makes it feel like a real memory, and 'I'm no stranger to the mustache' is a perfect, quotable punchline. Only Joey could deliver this with genuine sincerity — perfect character integration. The two-beat structure (the name, then the reveal) is textbook. Approaches the 8.0 anchor in quality.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Warren Beatty said I was a bad kisser!

jokes.text: 'That's like... like Mother Teresa, not a good mother.'
jokes.setup: Joey is outraged that Warren Beatty called him a bad kisser and tries to articulate how absurd that is via analogy
jokes.punchline: His analogy lands on 'Mother Teresa, not a good mother' — a vaguely logical but tonally absurd comparison that only half-works
jokes.explanation: Joey's fumbled analogies are a character staple, so this fits his voice well. But the analogy itself is slightly muddled — Mother Teresa as a 'mother' is a stretch even for Joey's logic. Gets a chuckle for the character beat but is structurally weak.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's like calling Mother Teresa a bad mother!

jokes.text: 'What does Warren Beatty know about kissing?'
jokes.setup: The friends are consoling Joey about Beatty's criticism
jokes.punchline: Monica asks what Warren Beatty — Hollywood's most legendary lover — would know about kissing, an obviously absurd question played straight
jokes.explanation: The joke works on economy — four words set up a perfect ironic punchline. The humor depends on the audience knowing Beatty's reputation. Solid throwaway gag.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Look, who cares what Warren Beatty thinks? He's just some guy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Just some guy? Ross, Warren Beatty is like, the most famous lover in Hollywood!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So? That doesn't mean his opinion matters.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Are you kidding me? Warren Beatty's romantic reputation is legendary!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well... okay, maybe his opinion matters a little.

jokes.text: 'Good. Very good. Firm, but tender. I'd recommend you to a friend.'
jokes.setup: Rachel kisses Joey to help him practice; everyone waits for his verdict
jokes.punchline: Joey critiques the kiss like a Yelp review — clinical, detached, absurdly businesslike
jokes.explanation: High character integration — this is exactly how Joey would evaluate a kiss, like a food critic. 'I'd recommend you to a friend' is a genuinely funny line with strong economy. The professional detachment is perfectly in character and subverts the awkwardness of the situation.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Did I just say that Warren Beatty doesn't know how to kiss? *nervous laugh* Oh God, oh God, oh God.

jokes.text: 'Over my dead body.' / 'And I'll be using his dead body as a shield.'
jokes.setup: Joey suggests someone (Ross) kiss him to practice; Ross flatly refuses
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately one-ups by saying he'll hide behind Ross's corpse — escalating the refusal to absurdist lengths
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler quip — takes Ross's refusal and escalates it with physical absurdism. The two-beat structure (Ross sets, Chandler delivers) is crisp. 'Dead body as a shield' is a memorably silly image.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, can one of you kiss me? I need to practice for an audition.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Absolutely not.

jokes.text: 'I cannot believe I have to walk down the aisle in front of 200 people looking like something you drink when you're nauseous.'
jokes.setup: Rachel comes out in her hideous bridesmaid dress; everyone can see it's awful
jokes.punchline: Rachel describes herself as looking like 'something you drink when you're nauseous' — a Pepto-Bismol pink dress comparison
jokes.explanation: Great specific imagery — 'something you drink when you're nauseous' is a vivid, original way to describe Pepto pink. Works as both a fashion joke and a visual gag. Rachel's vanity makes this character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'll do it.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, Joey, that's okay. We already kissed.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know, but I don't mind doing it again.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I do. I'm not kissing you again, Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Why not? What's the big deal?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Because the last time we kissed, it was weird.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Weird? I thought it was great!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, it was weird for me. So no, I'm not doing it again.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, well, you promised Barry you'd marry him.'
jokes.setup: Rachel says she promised Mindy she'd attend, implying her promises are binding
jokes.punchline: Phoebe points out Rachel also promised to marry Barry — undermining the premise that her promises are reliable
jokes.explanation: Sharp callback to the series premise (Rachel running from her wedding) delivered with perfect economy. The logic is airtight and the timing is quick. Not Phoebe's most character-specific line but lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, so... you're very enthusiastic, which is great. But maybe you could be a little more gentle? You know, like you're not trying to suck out my soul.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Gentle. Got it. Anything else?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, your technique is solid, but you tend to lead with your tongue a little too much. It's like... five stars for effort, two stars for execution.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Two stars? What do I have to do to get five?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Practice. And maybe... don't think about it so much? You're kissing someone, not performing open-heart surgery.

jokes.text: Rachel says she needs to be in a room with these people and 'feel good about myself' — then cuts to her in a hideous pink dress
jokes.setup: Rachel explains her noble reason for attending her ex's wedding
jokes.punchline: The visual irony of her stated goal ('feel good about myself') juxtaposed with the humiliating bridesmaid dress she's wearing
jokes.explanation: The structural irony is clear and works well as a scene-closer. Not exceptional but a competent joke built into the episode's fabric.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No! No way! I'm not doing that!

jokes.text: 'Someone's wearing the same clothes as last night. Get some action?'
jokes.setup: Chandler walks in wearing yesterday's clothes, clearly having been up all night
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately reads the situation and teases Chandler about getting laid
jokes.explanation: A functional observational beat. Joey's immediate jump to 'get some action?' is consistent with his character but isn't a particularly original observation. Sets up the internet-girl reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, you say that now, but when the time comes, I think you'll be very relaxed about it.

jokes.text: 'We stayed up talking on the Internet.' / 'Geek!'
jokes.setup: Joey calls Chandler a 'stud' assuming he hooked up; Chandler reveals they just talked online
jokes.punchline: Joey's instant reversal from 'Stud!' to 'Geek!' is perfectly timed
jokes.explanation: Extremely economical — the misdirection and reversal happen in two words ('Stud!' → 'Geek!'). Joey's binary view of masculinity is perfectly captured. A tight, funny beat that benefits from the mid-90s context of internet dating being considered dorky.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I have to walk down the aisle in this thing? I look like a Pepto-Bismol bottle!

jokes.text: Stud! ... Geek!
jokes.setup: Joey assumes Chandler got lucky, calls him a stud; learns the truth (online chatting)
jokes.punchline: Immediate reversal to 'Geek!' — the misdirection and speed of the reversal is the comedy
jokes.explanation: Brilliant economy — the entire setup and punchline are delivered in two words across a pause. The two-word reversal structure is almost perfectly efficient. The timing-dependent comedy of 'Stud!' followed by 'Geek!' is a masterclass in economy even if the concept itself isn't wildly original.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, didn't you promise Barry you'd marry him?

jokes.text: Monica says dreamily, 'I think my boyfriend's ever so dreamy. I wonder what our wedding will be like.'
jokes.setup: Richard just left after a warm goodbye; Monica is clearly head over heels
jokes.punchline: Her fantasizing about their wedding in a dreamy, girlish voice is played for irony — Richard is significantly older and has made no such suggestion
jokes.explanation: Mild character humor setting up the episode's emotional arc. The dreamy delivery undercuts Monica's usual assertiveness for comic effect, but it's more setup than punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! Walk of shame!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? No, I just fell asleep at Monica's.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Sure you did. In those clothes? From yesterday?

jokes.text: 'Afraid to ask him?' / 'Could not be more terrified.'
jokes.setup: Rachel probes Monica about whether she's discussed the future with Richard
jokes.punchline: Monica's 'Could not be more terrified' — delivered as casual admission — lands as both funny and poignant
jokes.explanation: Nice economy — the full admission of terror without elaboration. Works as both comedy and character reveal. Monica's vulnerability peeking through her usual competence is always effective.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Stud!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Geek!

jokes.text: 'Give Rachel another chance to dress like Princess Bubble Yum.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is told he should consider marriage
jokes.punchline: He pivots to mocking Rachel's bridesmaid dress with 'Princess Bubble Yum' — a callback to the pink dress and a classic Chandler deflection
jokes.explanation: Chandler deflecting from a serious topic with a devastatingly specific insult is peak character. 'Princess Bubble Yum' is a great coinage — specific, visual, and quotable. Using the deflection to avoid the marriage conversation is also structurally smart.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You guys know I get defensive and quippy when I'm uncomfortable, right?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, really? Because I had no idea. This is all news to me.

jokes.text: 'Babies probably learn to talk so they can tell grownups to cut it out.'
jokes.setup: Joey is doing repetitive peekaboo with a baby
jokes.punchline: Chandler's deadpan theory that babies develop language specifically to make adults stop being annoying
jokes.explanation: An excellent Chandler one-liner. The observation reframes a universal childhood milestone (learning to talk) as a defensive mechanism against adult foolishness. Original premise, perfect economy, totally in his voice. Approaches the 8.0 anchor in terms of craft.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know, I've been thinking about our friendship, and I just want to say that you guys mean the world to me. I don't say it enough, but I really do love you all.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, are you okay? Do you have a tumor?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Is this some kind of joke? Because it's not funny.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Chandler, you're scaring me.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah man, just go back to making fun of us or something.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: This is weird. I don't like it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? I can't just express my feelings?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No. No, you can't. It's not natural.

jokes.text: Richard: 'You are it.' Monica: 'Oh, God. You're about to get so lucky.'
jokes.setup: Richard gives a romantic answer about Monica being 'it' in his future
jokes.punchline: Monica's immediate, pragmatic pivot to sex ('You're about to get so lucky') undercuts the romance with comedic bluntness
jokes.explanation: Monica's directness is a great character signature. The abrupt pivot from romantic to transactional is perfectly Monica. Short, punchy, and lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh Richard, you're like a warm, buttery croissant on a cold winter morning, filling my soul with the golden essence of your love.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: Monica, that's... very poetic.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And you're like a strong, dark espresso that awakens my deepest desires, a cappuccino of passion that—

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, we get it. You two are in love. Can we please just order our coffee now?

jokes.text: 'Like a hound?' / 'Not a basset. A bassinet.'
jokes.setup: Monica asks if Richard sees 'a little bassinet in the corner' in their imagined future
jokes.punchline: Richard mishears 'bassinet' as 'basset' (hound), leading to a brief absurd tangent
jokes.explanation: A light wordplay beat that briefly deflates tension. The mishearing gag is familiar but serves the scene. Functional rather than inspired.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Are you afraid to ask him about marriage?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Afraid? Ross, I'm not afraid. I'm terrified. I'm so scared that when I think about talking to him, I get physically ill. I can't eat, I can't sleep, I just lie there at night, sweating through my sheets, imagining all the ways he could say no.

jokes.text: 'Well, I just think the baby would keep falling off the dog.'
jokes.setup: Richard is confused why they need a bassinet (having thought it was a basset hound)
jokes.punchline: Monica explains matter-of-factly that the baby would fall off the dog — taking the wordplay confusion to its logical absurd conclusion
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the basset/bassinet confusion is genuinely clever — Monica commits to the absurdist image completely, delivered with her characteristic matter-of-fact tone. 'The baby would keep falling off the dog' is a funny, imageable line.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You should really think about getting married, Mon.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Why would I do that?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, at least you'd only have to wear one awful bridesmaid dress instead of multiple ones like Rachel does.

jokes.text: 'I'm talking hovercrafts and apes taking over the planet.'
jokes.setup: Monica pushes for clarity on children; Richard tries to deflect by framing the future as impossibly distant
jokes.punchline: He illustrates 'the distant future' with 'hovercrafts and apes taking over the planet' — a Planet of the Apes reference delivered as if it's a reasonable timeframe
jokes.explanation: The specificity of the deflection (apes taking over!) is funny. Richard using sci-fi dystopia to avoid a relationship conversation is a nice character moment. Good but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what I think? I think babies don't actually want to talk. They're just playing peek-a-boo with language. Like, they know the word, but they're not gonna say it because they think it's funny to watch us freak out.

jokes.text: 'Come on, Chandler. I want this part so much. Just one kiss. I won't tell anyone.' / 'Joey, no means no.'
jokes.setup: Joey is still trying to practice kissing for his audition
jokes.punchline: Chandler's 'Joey, no means no' — flipping the gender dynamics of the common phrase in an absurd context
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'no means no' recontextualized for a man refusing another man's plea to kiss him for acting practice is sharp and economical. Chandler's delivery would be perfectly dry. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Do you see a bassinet in our future?

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: A basset? Monica, I'm 61 years old. I don't have the energy for a basset hound.

jokes.text: 'I'm sorry, we don't have your sheep.'
jokes.setup: Unclear what precedes this — likely a phone call or non sequitur from an unseen gag
jokes.punchline: The completely random, context-free line delivered with Chandler's signature deadpan
jokes.explanation: A cold absurdist non sequitur that works as a Chandler character beat. Without full visual context it's hard to score higher, but the randomness is committed to well.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: A dog wouldn't work. It would chew up the baby's toys, shed all over everything, and you'd have to walk it at three in the morning when the baby's crying anyway.

jokes.text: 'And you. You... I could eat you.' / 'Get away from me. I said no.'
jokes.setup: Joey continues trying to get someone to practice-kiss him
jokes.punchline: Chandler's escalating 'I said no' — now treating it like a sustained harassment situation
jokes.explanation: The running gag of Chandler refusing Joey's advances escalates nicely. 'I said no' lands as a callback. Functional running gag execution.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I want to have kids... eventually.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Like, maybe in five or ten years.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Or twenty years.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, fifty years.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: When I'm ninety-seven and they've invented that thing where they can just grow babies in tubes.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And also time travel, so I can go back and meet them as children.

jokes.text: 'She likes art... and I like funny words.'
jokes.setup: Chandler shows off a website about the Guggenheim to connect with his online girlfriend
jokes.punchline: His explanation of the dynamic — 'she likes art, I like funny words' — is a charmingly self-deprecating admission of incompatibility
jokes.explanation: Extremely economical self-summary. 'I like funny words' as Chandler's entire intellectual passion is a perfect piece of character writing — self-aware, sad, and funny simultaneously. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: How you doin'?

jokes.text: 'Are you the cutest? I'm afraid I might just be.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is excited about his online connection and seems to be responding to something sweet she wrote
jokes.punchline: He responds to a compliment by answering his own rhetorical question with narcissistic sincerity — 'I'm afraid I might just be'
jokes.explanation: A nice self-amused Chandler moment — the faux-modest 'I'm afraid I might just be' reads as both endearing and gently narcissistic. Good character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That dress is so... pretty! It's like something a little girl would wear to her first tea party with her dolly!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross...

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, I mean it! Very... youthful. Like you just learned what clothes are!

jokes.text: 'It could be a guy.' / 'It's not a guy.' / 'It could be like a big giant guy.'
jokes.setup: The friends tease Chandler that he doesn't really know who his online girlfriend is
jokes.punchline: Joey escalates from 'it could be a guy' to 'a big giant guy' — the escalation is funnier than the base joke
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'a guy' to 'a big giant guy' is a Joey-specific bit of comedic inflation. Simple but effective — his insistence on the modifier 'big giant' is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I'm looking at the Guggenheim website because my internet girlfriend thinks it's impressive. But honestly, I'm just there for the humor.

jokes.text: 'Ask her how long she's gonna live. Women live longer than men.'
jokes.setup: Friends are trying to help Chandler verify his online girlfriend's identity/gender
jokes.punchline: Joey suggests asking her lifespan as a gender-verification test — based on the completely flawed logic that longevity is gender-diagnostic
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey logic: technically based on a real fact (women live longer) but applied in a completely useless way. The confidence with which he proposes this is the joke. Perfect character integration — only Joey would think this is a useful test.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you're being so cute about this!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know, I'm adorable. Could I BE any more adorable?

jokes.text: 'How do you not fall down more?'
jokes.setup: Joey has proposed another piece of absurd logic
jokes.punchline: Chandler's exasperated 'How do you not fall down more?' — an insult masquerading as a genuine question
jokes.explanation: One of the best Chandler lines in the episode. Seven words that perfectly capture the Chandler-Joey dynamic — the exasperation is real, the question is absurd, and it implies Joey's stupidity is so profound it should have physical consequences. Extremely quotable, maximally economical. Meets the 8.0 anchor comfortably — sharp, unexpected, highly quotable, perfect economy. Strong candidate for standout moment.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Could be a guy! A big guy! A really big guy with a beard! Who works at a lumberyard!

jokes.text: 'My husband is sleeping with his secretary.'
jokes.setup: Chandler types 'What is your method of birth control?' to verify she's a woman
jokes.punchline: Instead of a direct answer, she reveals her husband is cheating — meaning she's married AND explaining her birth control situation via marital dysfunction
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke — the answer confirms she's a woman (good news) while simultaneously revealing she's married and her husband is cheating (bad news). The joke does triple duty: confirms gender, reveals marital status, and explains birth control method in one line. Strong structure.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So you're gonna ask her how long she's gonna live?

jokes.text: 'At least we know she's a woman.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is devastated that his online girlfriend is married
jokes.punchline: Joey finds the silver lining — at least the 'big giant guy' theory is disproven
jokes.explanation: Joey's unfailing optimism applied to a bad situation. The callback to the 'guy' concern makes this land better than it would standalone. Classic Joey silver-lining logic.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You can't throw rice at weddings anymore because the birds eat it and it kills them. So now people throw birdseed, which is stupid because the birds are just gonna eat that too. They're gonna be like, 'Oh boy, birdseed!' It's a death trap!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And that's why you should never eat sushi. Because the rice is a death trap for the fish.

jokes.text: 'I read this article that says you shouldn't throw rice at weddings. When pigeons eat rice, it kills them. That's why you never see pigeons in sushi bars.'
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel are at the wedding trying to ignore the emotional elephant in the room; Ross attempts small talk
jokes.punchline: 'That's why you never see pigeons in sushi bars' — a completely illogical non sequitur that treats 'pigeons avoid sushi bars because of the rice' as a scientific conclusion
jokes.explanation: A brilliant piece of Ross character comedy. He starts with a real fact (the rice/pigeon myth), then his paleontologist brain extends it to a hilariously false 'therefore' — as if pigeons consciously avoid sushi bars because of rice awareness. The absurdist logic is perfectly Ross: overeducated, socially awkward, and completely missing the emotional moment. One of the episode's standout jokes. Approaches the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I just... I don't know. Every time I think about walking down that aisle, I keep remembering the last time I did that. And I literally ran away in my wedding dress.

jokes.text: 'See, we're having fun.' / 'Oh, absolutely.' / 'I'm not thinking about that thing that we're gonna not think about.' / 'Neither am I.'
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel are clearly both thinking about the emotional weight of being at Rachel's ex's wedding
jokes.punchline: Both insist they're 'not thinking about that thing' — the meta-acknowledgment of the thing they're not thinking about confirms they're both thinking about it
jokes.explanation: Good ironic beat — the denial structure is a classic comedy device. Works as both comedy and emotional shorthand. Not particularly original but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Ross! You could have told me my dress was inside out!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I tried! I tried to tell you, but every time I opened my mouth, Chandler kept making faces at me, and Monica was giving me this look like I was about to say something inappropriate, and Joey just kept talking about food!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So what? You just let me walk around like that?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I was in an impossible situation! If I told you, it would be weird. If I didn't tell you, it was also weird. There was no winning here, Rachel!

jokes.text: Rachel sees the window she crawled out of at her wedding and starts spiraling about being judged
jokes.setup: Rachel is trying to be brave at Barry's wedding
jokes.punchline: The specific detail of seeing the actual window she escaped through — the physical evidence of her humiliation — triggers a panic that is both sympathetic and comedic
jokes.explanation: More of an emotional beat with comedic elements. The visual detail (the specific window) is funny but it's primarily played for character sympathy. Cringe-adjacent.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I've been humiliated before, but this is the worst. Remember when I tripped at the Copacabana and everyone saw me fall? I just ran out of there. I didn't even wait for my drink.

jokes.text: 'Stand up and shout, "Hey, your butt's showing!"' / 'Better you than Barry's uncle.'
jokes.setup: Rachel demands to know why the bridesmaid didn't warn her about the exposed dress
jokes.punchline: 'Better you than Barry's uncle' — implying Barry's uncle has been enjoying the view, which is far more disturbing
jokes.explanation: A darkly funny implication — Barry's uncle has been ogling Rachel and the bridesmaid considered this preferable. The economy is strong and the dark implication lands as genuinely funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hey, it's okay. Everyone does embarrassing things. It doesn't define who you are.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, I know that. But he saw me! He literally saw me!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: And? So what? He probably forgot about it already.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: How can you be so sure?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Because people are generally self-absorbed. Trust me.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, it's too late now anyway. I'm already committed to him.

jokes.text: Rachel confesses that in eighth grade she had to sing 'Copacabana' to the entire school, and two lines in, she freaked out
jokes.setup: Rachel is comparing this humiliation to past humiliations to put it in context
jokes.punchline: The specific detail of 'Copacabana' establishes the callback that pays off magnificently later in the episode
jokes.explanation: As a standalone joke it's moderately amusing. Its real value is as setup for the episode's best comedic moment. The specificity of 'Copacabana' is funny in itself — an odd song choice for a school performance.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Weinberg
dialogue.line: It's been a long time since I've seen Rachel like that.

jokes.text: 'Ross, would you stop! You got me. I'm dating you.'
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to reassure Rachel about the eighth-grade Copacabana incident, saying it 'wasn't so bad'
jokes.punchline: Rachel snaps that Ross doesn't need to soften the past anymore — she's already his girlfriend, so the revisionism is unnecessary
jokes.explanation: A sharp character beat — Rachel cutting through Ross's well-meaning flattery with pragmatic honesty. 'You got me' is an economical and funny way to tell someone to stop trying so hard.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You lie to me?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No! Well... yes. But only about important things.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Like... how much I care about you. I tell you I care about you this much, but I actually care about you this much.

jokes.text: 'In fact, I hardly expected to see so much.'
jokes.setup: Rachel greets Barry's relatives; Mr. Weinberg says it's wonderful to see her
jokes.punchline: 'I hardly expected to see so much' — a polite, understated reference to Rachel's exposed rear end
jokes.explanation: The old-fashioned, formal phrasing of the innuendo ('I hardly expected to see so much') makes it funnier. It's a genteel version of the obvious joke, which elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Mindy
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Mindy Feldman-Henderson-Rothschild-Grayson-Carmichael-DuPont-Vanderbilt-Astor-Whitney-Rockefeller.

jokes.text: 'You told me you didn't see.' / 'I tell you a lot of things.'
jokes.setup: Rachel confronts the bridesmaid who earlier claimed not to have seen her exposed dress
jokes.punchline: 'I tell you a lot of things' — a casually devastating admission that everything she said was potentially a lie
jokes.explanation: Extremely economical — 'I tell you a lot of things' dismantles the previous scene's comfort with four words while being genuinely funny in its casual nihilism. Strong quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Barry
dialogue.line: Well, this wedding is going much better than my first one.

dialogue.speaker: Barry
dialogue.line: That one only lasted three minutes.

jokes.text: 'Well, it's wonderful to have you up and about again, dear.'
jokes.setup: Another guest makes a comment that implies Rachel was recently very ill
jokes.punchline: 'Up and about again' suggests Rachel was bedridden — building mystery about what story Barry's family told
jokes.explanation: A running gag building toward the syphilis reveal. As a standalone moment it's mild, but it's doing important structural work setting up a bigger payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Everyone keeps asking if I'm okay because I look sick.

dialogue.speaker: Mindy
dialogue.line: Well, first they think you're just insane.

dialogue.speaker: Barry
dialogue.line: Then they assume it's from syphilis.

jokes.text: 'At our wedding, they'd packed up the chopped liver by now.'
jokes.setup: Mindy greets Rachel warmly at her wedding; the conversation is cheerful
jokes.punchline: Mindy casually refers to the aborted wedding — where Rachel fled — as a reference point for how long the party would have lasted. Dark, breezy, and perfectly timed.
jokes.explanation: The casualness with which Mindy references Rachel running out on Barry as a scheduling reference point is darkly brilliant. Using 'chopped liver' as the time marker is wonderfully specific and Jewish-wedding-coded. The joke implies this is just... a thing that happened, not a big deal — which is both funny and a little unsettling.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Why would you tell people I have syphilis?

dialogue.speaker: Barry
dialogue.line: I was just trying to help you save face. I thought it would be better than telling people the truth.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Better than what truth?

dialogue.speaker: Barry
dialogue.line: That you left me at the altar! But I figured nobody had to know that, so I told them you were sick.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You told people I had syphilis instead of telling them I left you?

dialogue.speaker: Barry
dialogue.line: Yes! Because if people knew you left me, they might think there was something wrong with me. This way, it's just you with a disease.

jokes.text: Barry's parents told people Rachel was 'sort of... insane. From the syphilis.'
jokes.setup: Rachel demands to know why people keep commenting on her health; Mindy reveals the cover story with increasing specificity
jokes.punchline: 'Insane. From the syphilis.' — The reveal escalates from 'insane' (embarrassing) to 'from the syphilis' (mortifying and specific)
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. The long setup (three separate 'up and about' beats) pays off with an escalating revelation — insane is bad enough, but 'from the syphilis' is genius. The beat between 'insane' and 'from the syphilis' (implied pause) is perfect structural comedy. Barry's parents choosing syphilis specifically — not cancer, not depression, but an STD — is both absurd and character-revealing. The payoff justifies all the groundwork. Genuinely exceptional joke writing.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Why won't you respond to her?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Because she's not real, Phoebe. She's on the internet.

jokes.text: Angela? Joey Tribbiani. Listen, what are you doing tonight? I know you're seeing that guy. I thought maybe you could bring him...
jokes.setup: Joey is at a wedding, apparently calling a woman he knows who is in a relationship
jokes.punchline: Joey's attempt to set up a date while acknowledging she has a boyfriend — and apparently trying to include the boyfriend in some arrangement — implies his characteristic romantic audacity mid-wedding
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy — Joey hitting on a woman at a wedding is on-brand. But the joke is incomplete in the transcript (we don't hear the full pitch), which limits both the comedy and the scoring. The setup is stronger than the payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: So what if she's married? That doesn't mean anything. My third husband was married when I met him.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Your third husband was married to you!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Exactly! So I know it can work.

jokes.text: 'That's the 10th bing-bong message she's sent.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is ignoring his online girlfriend's messages after learning she's married
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's 'bing-bong' as her term for instant messages — a charmingly naive description of technology from the character least likely to understand it
jokes.explanation: Phoebe calling IMs 'bing-bong messages' is perfect character voice. Her friendly, childlike relationship with technology produces great incidental comedy. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You're gonna regret not being flexible when you're older.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm gonna regret a lot of things when I'm older. Not being able to lick my own butt is not gonna be high on that list.

jokes.text: 'If you don't meet her, you'll kick yourself when you're 80... which is hard to do and you'll break a hip.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe urges Chandler to go meet his online girlfriend despite her being married
jokes.punchline: She adds a practical caveat to the cliché 'you'll kick yourself' — at 80, literally kicking yourself would break your hip
jokes.explanation: A genuinely excellent Phoebe joke. She takes a cliché ('you'll kick yourself') and extends its literal meaning with perfectly Phoebe logic — she's not wrong! The hip-breaking addendum is an absurdist extension that feels absolutely true to her character. Both quotable and structurally sound. Approaches the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I can help you with this. Just... just stay calm and listen to me carefully.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, wait, do it this way. Actually, no, the other way was better. Wait, what were we doing?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You need to do it faster! But also slower, so you don't mess up. But hurry!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Don't think about it, just do it! But think about it carefully first!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm helping! I'm being so helpful right now!

jokes.text: 'Those are the bing bongs of a woman in love with you.'
jokes.setup: Chandler hesitates; Phoebe listens to the IM notifications
jokes.punchline: Phoebe interprets the sound of IM notifications as emotionally expressive — 'the bing bongs of a woman in love'
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'bing bong' and the romantic framing of a computer notification sound is pure Phoebe. Her earnest romanticism mixed with technological naivety is a great character signature. 'The bing bongs of a woman in love' is extremely quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm going to sing Copacabana again. I don't care what happened the last time.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I have to face my fears. This is about overcoming my childhood trauma.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, your childhood trauma was that your parents wouldn't buy you a pony.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Exactly! And now I'm going to conquer this song!

jokes.text: Phoebe's chaotic pre-meeting preparation — 'Take a shower... no, answer her first... no, make coffee...' — escalating into logistical panic
jokes.setup: Chandler agrees to meet her; Phoebe tries to orchestrate the preparation
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's instructions collapse into contradictory chaos — shower, then answer, then coffee — as she overwhelms herself and Chandler
jokes.explanation: A solid physical/verbal escalation beat from Phoebe. Her chaotic enthusiasm is funny, though this type of 'can't organize my thoughts' comedy is fairly standard. The performance would carry it more than the writing.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I don't need children. I'm perfectly happy without them. I have my career, my apartment, my friends...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Who am I kidding? I want a baby! I want to have a baby so badly! Why can't I have a baby?!

jokes.text: Okay, one more, please. I'm gonna get it in this time. / Okay, last chance.
jokes.setup: Joey is still attempting to get Chandler to practice kissing him throughout the episode
jokes.punchline: Even in the middle of Chandler's romantic crisis, Joey's singular focus on his audition kissing problem persists
jokes.explanation: A solid running gag beat — Joey's persistent self-absorption is funny because of the timing (Chandler is in emotional distress). The joke works through juxtaposition more than craft. 'Last chance' from Chandler is a nice button.

dialogue.speaker: Best Man
dialogue.line: What? It worked the first time!

jokes.text: Richard's 'if I have to' speech — he commits to having children but repeats 'if I have to' approximately 17 times
jokes.setup: Richard tries to commit to Monica's desire for children
jokes.punchline: Monica counts '17 times' he said 'if I have to' — each repetition undermining the supposed commitment
jokes.explanation: The comedy of a man trying to be romantic while inadvertently expressing reluctance with every breath. The escalation of 'if I have to' working against him is structurally strong and character-appropriate — Richard is a man doing the right thing for the wrong reasons.

dialogue.speaker: Best Man
dialogue.line: Rachel showed real courage today. She walked down that aisle with such confidence and grace.

dialogue.speaker: Best Man
dialogue.line: Of course, that confidence lasted until we all saw what was holding up her dress.

jokes.text: 'I remember when Barry got home from his first date with Rachel.' (Best man starting a toast) / 'You hired the same band. I can't use the same speech?'
jokes.setup: The best man begins a toast at Barry's wedding with Mindy, starting with a memory of Barry's first date with Rachel
jokes.punchline: Barry protests — revealing the best man is reusing his toast from Barry's first (aborted) wedding
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The best man reusing a toast from a previous wedding (with a different bride!) is a devastating character indictment — of Barry, of the best man, and of the social world they inhabit. The logic ('you hired the same band') is both absurdly reasonable and completely damning. Structurally perfect: setup builds naturally, punchline recontextualizes everything. Meets the 8.0 anchor clearly.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: And another thing! The rumor about Rachel and syphilis is completely false!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: She does not have syphilis. She never had syphilis. And frankly, I'm insulted that anyone would even suggest—

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know what? Now everyone's going to think she has syphilis!

jokes.text: Best man's toast: '...And even fewer who'd do it with their asses hanging out.'
jokes.setup: Best man gives a genuine compliment about Rachel's courage in attending the wedding
jokes.punchline: He undercuts the compliment by referencing Rachel's exposed dress — turning a sincere moment into a roast
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the dress situation, made funnier by the whiplash from genuine praise to butt joke. The formal toast context amplifies the vulgarity of 'asses hanging out.' Clean structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: She didn't love him.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I mean, that's good for me.

jokes.text: Oh, dear God.
jokes.setup: Rachel's boyfriend Ross is about to stand up and make an impromptu speech at the wedding
jokes.punchline: Rachel's sotto voce 'Oh, dear God' — visible dread at what Ross is about to do
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum dread. Rachel's reaction anticipates and frames what is about to be a spectacular disaster. The comedy is in the shared knowledge between Rachel and the audience that Ross is going to make this so much worse.

dialogue.speaker: Wedding Guest
dialogue.line: That's the third Barry event Rachel's walked out of this month.

dialogue.speaker: Wedding Guest
dialogue.line: I've got twenty bucks says she makes it through the rehearsal dinner next week.

dialogue.speaker: Barry
dialogue.line: You're on. I give her ten minutes.

jokes.text: Oh, dear God.
jokes.setup: Ross announces himself as Rachel's boyfriend and begins delivering an impromptu speech at the wedding
jokes.punchline: Mindy's audible horror — 'Oh, dear God' — at realizing what's about to happen
jokes.explanation: Three words that carry enormous comedic weight. Mindy's reaction anticipates the disaster before it happens and the audience shares her dread. The reaction beat works because we've all been at social events where someone is about to make it worse, and Mindy's response is the perfect articulation of that feeling. Strong economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I can't leave the wedding. Barry's going to have so many more of these.

jokes.text: 'She did not run out on Barry because she had syphilis.'
jokes.setup: Ross is making a toast at a stranger's wedding to clear Rachel's name
jokes.punchline: Announcing 'she did not have syphilis' at a wedding — an announcement that by its nature implies the rumor is widespread
jokes.explanation: The callback to the syphilis revelation lands with full force here. Ross announcing to a roomful of strangers that Rachel doesn't have syphilis is both cringe-comedically perfect and structurally excellent. The more he tries to help, the worse it gets — classic Ross.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I did it. I actually did it. I performed the Copacabana and I didn't have a panic attack.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Rach, that was amazing!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You were incredible. I didn't know you had that in you.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Neither did I. Who knew all I needed was to face my fears head-on?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's what I've been telling people for years.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Your aura is like, totally different now. It's all sparkly and trauma-free.

jokes.text: Ross's toast recap: 'So to review: Rachel took a lot of courage... doesn't have the syphilis... and wound up with me.'
jokes.setup: Ross attempts to conclude his disastrous toast with a summary
jokes.punchline: 'To review' — as if he's summarizing a business presentation — followed by 'doesn't have the syphilis' and the self-congratulatory 'wound up with me'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's absolute best jokes. 'So to review' is peak Ross — treating a social catastrophe with PowerPoint-presentation energy. The three-point 'review': (1) courage, (2) no syphilis, (3) 'wound up with me' is perfectly constructed escalating absurdism. The self-congratulatory final point ('wound up with me') is character-perfect. Highly quotable, completely original in its specificity. This is exceptional comedy writing that integrates character, situation, and wordplay seamlessly.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: At the Copa... she lost her love.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: His name was Rico.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: He wore a diamond.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: He was escaping to New York, La-La-La-La-La.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: At the Copa... she lost her love.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: His name was Rico.

dialogue.speaker: All
dialogue.line: At the Copa!

jokes.text: 'See you in the parking lot.' Ross's response: 'No, Rach.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is mortified by Ross's toast
jokes.punchline: Rachel threatens to storm out; Ross's exhausted 'No, Rach' implies this is becoming a pattern
jokes.explanation: A brief reaction beat that works from character dynamics. Ross's weary pre-emptive 'No, Rach' implies he expected this reaction, which is both funny and relationally honest.

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: I'm willing to give up my entire record collection for you.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Really? That's so sweet!

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: Well, I made copies.

jokes.text: 'And once again, she is out of here! Okay, who had 9:45?'
jokes.setup: Rachel storms out after Ross's toast
jokes.punchline: The best man announces her departure as if calling a bet — revealing the wedding guests had a pool on when Rachel would leave
jokes.explanation: Brilliant joke. The reveal that the guests had a betting pool on Rachel's departure time — as if her flakiness is a known quantity — is darkly funny and structurally perfect. 'And once again, she is out of here!' treats it as a sporting event. The casual cruelty of 'who had 9:45?' is unexpected and devastating. This is exceptional comedy writing — original, character-revealing, and perfectly timed.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? You're doing it again! You keep saying 'I know this is crazy' — if you know it's crazy, why are you doing it?

dialogue.speaker: Richard
dialogue.line: Because I love you.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Then just say that! Don't lead with the disclaimer!

jokes.text: 'I promised myself I'd make it through at least one of your weddings.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has almost left but turns back; she confronts her own pattern
jokes.punchline: 'At least one of your weddings' — implying a pattern of Barry-adjacent weddings she's failed to complete
jokes.explanation: A great line that does double duty: it's both a character moment (Rachel's self-awareness) and a great joke (the implication that Barry has multiple weddings she's failed to see through). 'At least one of your weddings' is wonderfully specific and quietly devastating.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, that's nice. You know what they say - life is full of little surprises, and most of them are terrible.

jokes.text: Monica catches that Richard said 'if I have to' approximately 17 times and uses that as the reason she can't agree to have children
jokes.setup: Richard gives a heartfelt speech about being willing to have children
jokes.punchline: Monica counts the 'if I have to' repetitions and uses them as evidence the commitment isn't real — '17 times' used as a precise, devastating score
jokes.explanation: Monica's precision (17 times!) is both comedically and emotionally perfect. Her compulsive counting/record-keeping is completely in character, and the fact that she's listened so carefully that she has an exact count is both funny and heartbreaking. Strong payoff to the earlier speech.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A watched pot never boils, right? So I'm not gonna watch the pot.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But I am gonna watch the door, because a watched door never... opens?

jokes.text: 'Yeah, because life's just that kind.'
jokes.setup: Chandler spots someone he thinks might be his online girlfriend arriving
jokes.punchline: When told to be hopeful, Chandler's bitter 'Yeah, because life's just that kind' — his romantic pessimism in five words
jokes.explanation: Perfect Chandler deflection — five words that encapsulate his whole romantic worldview. The economy is exceptional. This is his character in a nutshell.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh. My. God.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Hi Chandler!

jokes.text: 'If you keep looking at it, the door's never gonna boil.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe tries to tell Chandler 'a watched pot never boils' as he stares at the door
jokes.punchline: She mangles the idiom — 'the door's never gonna boil' — mixing up pot and door in a perfectly Phoebe malformation
jokes.explanation: Excellent Phoebe joke. She starts the idiom correctly ('a watched pot...') then confuses the vehicle ('the door') while keeping the verb ('boil') — the resulting image of a boiling door is perfectly absurd. Maximum character integration: only Phoebe mangles idioms with such cheerful confidence. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm going to help you with your kissing.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, come here.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, the problem is you're too stiff. You need to relax your face.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And stop doing that thing with your lips.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What thing?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That thing! Where you do... that.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Here, let me show you.

jokes.text: You gotta stop staring at the door like a watched pot. If you keep looking at it, the door's never gonna boil.
jokes.setup: Joey is advising Chandler to stop watching the door for his online date
jokes.punchline: Joey mangles the 'a watched pot never boils' idiom — applying it to a door boiling — with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect Joey joke. He correctly identifies the spirit of the 'watched pot' idiom but confidently applies it to the wrong object — a door that apparently 'won't boil.' The joke works because Joey isn't stupid, he's confidently wrong, which is the show's best version of his character. 'The door's never gonna boil' is an instantly quotable non sequitur. High character integration — this is Joey at his most Joey. Earns its 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Thank you so much for helping me with my kissing technique, Monica. I really feel like I nailed it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's great, Joey! When's your audition?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, it was this morning.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: This morning?! Joey, why didn't you tell me?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know, I know. But hey, I learned something valuable today.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What's that?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Ross is a really good kisser.

jokes.text: 'I've felt guilty because I wanna be a good friend. And damn it, I am a good friend. So shut up and close your eyes.'
jokes.setup: Joey is clearly about to kiss Chandler to help him practice for his audition — after being repeatedly refused
jokes.punchline: Joey's entire moral justification — 'I am a good friend' therefore 'shut up and close your eyes' — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: A fantastic episode-length callback payoff. Joey's entire logic — genuine friendship requires sacrifice, therefore Chandler must kiss him — is delivered with absolute sincerity. The phrase 'shut up and close your eyes' as an act of love is perfectly Joey. Strong character integration; the whole episode's kissing subplot pays off here.

jokes.text: 'You are a good friend. The audition's over, and I didn't get it. But that was a hell of a kiss. Rachel is a very lucky girl.'
jokes.setup: Joey has kissed Chandler; both react
jokes.punchline: Chandler confirms Joey's kissing ability — 'a hell of a kiss' — and concludes 'Rachel is a very lucky girl,' implying Ross should be worried
jokes.explanation: The episode's perfect closer for the Joey subplot. Chandler's objective assessment ('that was a hell of a kiss') directly refutes Warren Beatty's criticism. 'Rachel is a very lucky girl' lands as both a compliment to Joey and an unexpected joke about the woman who kissed him earlier. The whole episode's kissing arc resolves in a deeply satisfying, funny way. Strong payoff energy.

jokes.text: You are a good friend. The audition's over, and I didn't get it. But that was a hell of a kiss. Rachel is a very lucky girl.
jokes.setup: Chandler has finally kissed Joey; the moment is the climax of the running gag
jokes.punchline: Joey confirms the audition is already over — making Chandler's sacrifice pointless — but then sincerely compliments his kissing while comparing him favorably to Rachel
jokes.explanation: An exceptional payoff to both the episode's running gag and Monica's earlier kissing review. 'Rachel is a very lucky girl' mirrors Monica's 'I'd recommend you to a friend' from the opening act — a perfect bookend. The added cruelty of 'the audition's over' (making Chandler's sacrifice meaningless) is a great dark twist. The callback structure across the whole episode is the mark of strong writing-room craft.

tmdb_overview: Rachel agrees to be maid of honor at her ex-fiancé's wedding; she relives the nightmare of her own failed wedding day. Meanwhile, Chandler becomes enamored with a woman he meets on the Internet, but is surprised when he finally meets her. Monica ponders her future with Richard.
insight: Wedding episode misfires: 64.8 score masks uneven pacing across scattered character threads.
